title: Keeping Doors Open
coreMove: Let a low-value option close so attention can move to the choice that actually matters.
sourcePressure: The source shows that people spend time, money, and attention preserving options even when the preservation cost exceeds the option's likely value.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says focus is good; the chapter-specific move is to calculate the active cost of keeping an option alive.

hook: Keeping choices alive costs more than losing them

exampleSpecs.domain: indie game studio maintaining three prototypes
exampleSpecs.audience: a two-person studio deciding which demo to stop updating
exampleSpecs.stakes: burning launch runway on keeping all prototypes playable for investors
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the studio deletes two prototype build slots from the weekly test calendar and watches the remaining demo get a real polish pass
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three game builds listed on a cracked whiteboard beside a countdown to demo day

exampleSpecs.domain: regional theater choosing scripts for a small season
exampleSpecs.audience: an artistic director holding options on too many productions
exampleSpecs.stakes: losing rehearsal quality because deposits keep every script technically alive
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director totals option fees and rehearsal conflicts on the lobby floor, then releases two scripts before casting begins
exampleSpecs.firstImage: script packets spread across a dark lobby carpet after closing night

exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer deciding whether to maintain credentials for animals she rarely handles
exampleSpecs.stakes: spending weekends on renewals instead of deepening skill for the species arriving daily
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she places the renewal forms beside the intake log and crosses out the certifications that served no animal in the last year
exampleSpecs.firstImage: renewal forms tucked under a clipboard of injured songbird intakes

exampleSpecs.domain: specialty coffee roaster carrying too many seasonal beans
exampleSpecs.audience: a roaster deciding which micro-lots to keep offering
exampleSpecs.stakes: wasting roast attention and inventory freshness by preserving a long menu
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the roaster tips the last stale beans from three low-volume jars and writes the freshness cost next to each kept option
exampleSpecs.firstImage: glass sample jars of green coffee lined beneath a roasting curve printout

exampleSpecs.domain: nonprofit grant calendar with too many possible applications
exampleSpecs.audience: a development director protecting staff time
exampleSpecs.stakes: submitting weak proposals because every grant door feels too risky to close
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director removes the lowest-fit grants from the wall calendar during the staff meeting and assigns saved hours to one high-fit proposal
exampleSpecs.firstImage: colored grant cards pinned across a wall calendar with strings between dates

exampleSpecs.audience: a culinary apprentice trying to keep every station path open
exampleSpecs.stakes: remaining mediocre across stations instead of becoming trusted on one critical station
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after missing prep on two stations, the apprentice gives up the least valuable rotation slot and spends the hour mastering fish butchery
exampleSpecs.firstImage: station cards clipped above a stainless prep table before service

skillTargets: calculate the maintenance cost of an open option
distinguish useful flexibility from option hoarding
choose which door to close based on actual use
explain why preserving possibilities can damage the main path

tryThisNowSpec: Name one option you are paying to keep alive with time or attention, then schedule a specific closing action unless it has been used in the last month.
